# Introduction

Plasma physics sits at the crossroads of kinetic theory, electromagnetism, fluid dynamics, and statistical mechanics. Nearly 99 % of the visible universe is in the plasma state, and laboratory plasmas underpin technologies ranging from fluorescent lighting to next‑generation accelerators and fusion‑energy concepts. This online book is an introduction to plasma physics from the point of view of transport, lasers and non-local theory. While there are many good introductory textbooks on plasma physics theory, herein the focus is on the practical aspects of plasma physics, with an emphasis on transport phenomena and the use of lasers in plasma experiments: the regimes of high-energy-density physics (HED). Such conditions are routinely accessed at facilities like the National Ignition Facility (NIF), OMEGA, and the Laser Mégajoule (LMJ), where nanosecond laser pulses generate plasmas exceeding tens of mega‑kelvin and magnetic fields of several tens of Tesla. It is therefore not a comprehensive textbook on plasma physics, but rather a resource for those interested in the applications of plasma physics in the context of laser-plasma interactions and transport phenomena.

The book is structured to provide a comprehensive overview of the key concepts and applications in plasma physics. The material is intended for senior undergraduates, graduate students, and early‑career researchers in physics or engineering who have a working knowledge of electrodynamics, statistical mechanics, and vector calculus. The content is designed to be accessible to students and researchers who may not have a deep background in plasma physics but are interested in its applications in the regime of collisional and magnetised plasmas, particularly in the context of HED physics.

In @sec-mhd we introduce the basic concepts of plasma kinetic theory and the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equation, from which we derive the equations of magneto-hydrodynamics (MHD): the theory of electrically conducting fluids in the presence of magnetic fields. This is a fundamental aspect of plasma physics, as it describes how plasmas interact with magnetic fields and how these interactions can lead to various phenomena such as magnetic confinement and plasma instabilities. In @sec-collisions we derive the collision operator for plasmas, and how this operator can be used to describe the transport of particles, momentum and energy in plasmas. Collisional processes in plasmas also allow us to introduce the closure of the fluid equations and derive the expressions for thermal transport and Ohm's law. @sec-transport builds on the previous chapter to introduce the transport coefficients and how they can be used to describe the anisotropic transport of particles, momentum and energy in plasmas in the presence of magnetic fields. This chapter further discusses important transport processes and phenomena that occur in the collisional and magnetised regime. When the electron distribution in a plasma is significantly far from a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, the local transport approximation breaks down and one must incorporate new models to explain non-local transport. When collisional mean‑free paths approach macroscopic scale‑lengths, classical transport fails. @sec-nonlocal introduces non-local transport theory and several models that implement corrections to standard local MHD. This chapter also discusses the limitations of the local transport approximation and how non-local transport theory can provide a more accurate description of plasma behaviour in certain regimes. 

The focus of this book is also the application of plasma physics in the context of laser-plasma interactions. In @sec-lasers we introduce some of the basic principles of laser propagation relevant to their interactions with plasmas. @sec-laserplasma will then discuss the interaction of lasers with plasmas, including the mechanisms of energy transfer and the effects of laser-plasma interactions on plasma behaviour. This chapter will also cover some of the important instabilities and phenomena that can arise in laser-plasma interactions, such as stimulated Raman scattering. In @sec-applications, we will explore some of the practical applications of plasma physics in the context of laser-plasma interactions, including inertial confinement fusion. This chapter will highlight the importance of plasma physics in advancing our understanding of fundamental physical processes.

I hope this focused approach helps readers build a familiarity with the background and physics required for understanding laser‑driven plasma physics. If you want to go further, there is a list of additional resources and books in @sec-summary. Plasma physics is a field that covers a wide range of phenomena, processes and theoretical and computational challenges that still remain relevant and exciting today. What begins as a simple kinetic theory of charged particles can lead to a rich and complex description of this remarkable state of matter.
